newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: PCIBank says not hit by ownership row.
newsitem.headline: PCIBank says not hit by ownership row.

text.p: PCIBank of the Philippines held its first shareholders meeting in more than four years on Friday, but a row lingered over sequestered shares that belonged to a relative of former president Ferdinand Marcos.

Officials said PCIBank, one of the largest banks in the country, was poised for further growth and was focusing on the growing middle-income market, but the meeting was mostly taken up with the dispute over the sequestered shares.
Rafael Buenaventura, president and chief executive officer, said the long-drawn out dispute, which started in the late 1980s, had not affected PCIBank's business.
"The dispute is for only one board seat... That's the whole irony of it," he told reporters after the meeting, which was delayed by bickering between lawyers.
The shareholders meeting was held for the first time since 1992 after the Supreme Court ruled in December that a general body meeting could be held to fill vacant seats on the board.
But it has barred those meeting from conducting any other business until the ownership of the sequestered shares is resolved.

Attorneys for Trans Middle East (Philippines) Equities Inc, which owned about 10.5 percent of the bank's outstanding shares, claimed that the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) had blocked the government's Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG) from exercising the voting rights attached to the shares.
The PCGG has sequestered the shares on suspicion that the owner of Trans Middle East, the brother of former first lady Imelda Marcos, had used illegally-gathered funds to purchase the stake.

PCGG is a government body tasked to recover all ill-gotten wealth of former strongman Marcos and his business associates. Marcos was ousted from the presidency in 1986 after 20 years in power and died in exile in 1989.
Lawyers for PCGG said the Supreme Court had allowed it to vote on behalf of the sequestered shares until the issue of real ownership is resolved by an anti-graft court.
Voting was ultimately held to fill places on the board, although lawyers for Trans Middle East said they would appeal to the Supreme Court to cancel the process.

The ongoing legal battle has, however, restricted PCIBank from acting on a plan to increase its capital, raise the ratio of foreign ownership to 40 percent from the present 30 percent, and declare a 50 percent to 100 percent stock dividend.
Despite this, Buenaventure said the bank still has some two billion pesos worth of unissued authorised shares which it could sell, possibly within this year.
He added that the bank is talking with several local banks for a possible merger.
Buenaventure said the bank's net income grew by 16.9 percent last year to 2.8 billion pesos from 2.395 billion registered the previous year.
He said the bank would concentrate on the middle-income market which has been expanding in tandem with the overall economy.
"We will continue to go for the middle market which is very buoyant," he added.
